Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

## Framework and conventions

- **XCTest only** — every file does `import XCTest` / `@testable import AlmanacCore`, `final class XTests: XCTestCase`. No `import Testing` (Swift Testing) anywhere.
- Test methods: `func testDescriptiveSentenceCase()`, e.g. `testDSTSpringForwardDayIsShorterThan24Hours`, `testStaleReimportDoesNotBecomeCurrent`. Names read as full sentences describing the behavior/assertion, not `test_snake_case`.
- Heavy use of doc comments above the `final class` explaining *why* the file exists (design-rationale style), and inline `//` comments on individual assertions explaining the specific edge case being pinned.
- Fixture pattern: a private `fixture()`/`migrated()` helper builds an in-memory `Database.inMemory()`, runs `MigrationRunner(migrations: AlmanacMigrations.all).migrate(db)`, and constructs the store under test with a `FixedClock`.
- On-disk DB tests (`ManualEntryTests`, `SyncAndBackupTests`, `MigrationRunnerTests`, `NutritionBundleImportTests`) use `NSTemporaryDirectory() + "almanac-<name>-\(UUID().uuidString).sqlite"` with `override func tearDown()` cleanup of the file plus `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars.
- `async throws` test functions are used (7 occurrences) for the `FakeHealthProvider`/HealthKit-async-style APIs, e.g. `testFakeHealthProviderRequiresAuthorisation() async throws`.
- Numbered inline comments (`// 1. ...`, `// 9. ...`) are used in some longer files (`LaboratoryTests.swift`, `TimelineTests.swift`) to track scenario coverage against a spec.

## Date/time/timezone/calendar tests already present

All concentrated in `Tests/AlmanacCoreTests/TimeModelTests.swift` (67 lines, testing `Sources/AlmanacCore/Time/TimeModel.swift`):

- `testRiyadhMidnightBoundary` — UTC-to-Asia/Riyadh (UTC+3, no DST) midnight boundary crossing.
- `testWakeOffsetPullsSmallHoursIntoPreviousDay` — a `.wakeOffset(hours: 4)` day-boundary rule pulling 01:30–03:59 into the previous logical day.
- `testBoundsAreHalfOpenAndRoundTrip` — half-open `[start, end)` day bounds.
- `testDSTSpringForwardDayIsShorterThan24Hours`:
  ```swift
  let tm = TimeModel(timeZone: TimeZone(identifier: "Europe/London")!)
  let b = tm.bounds(of: LogicalDay("2026-03-29"))!   // BST begins
  XCTAssertEqual(b.end.timeIntervalSince(b.start), 23 * 3600, accuracy: 1)
  ```
- `testDSTFallBackDayIsLongerThan24Hours` — same pattern for `2026-10-25` (BST ends), asserting 25 hours.
- `testEveryDayOfAYearRoundTrips` — walks all 365 days of 2026 in Riyadh with a wake-offset boundary, asserting `logicalDay(start)` and `logicalDay(end - 1s)` both map back to the same `LogicalDay`. **Note: 2026 is not a leap year, so this doesn't exercise Feb 29 — a leap-year variant (e.g. 2028) would be a natural extension.**

No other file references `TimeZone(identifier:` explicitly; `Europe/London` and `Asia/Riyadh` are the only two zones exercised in tests. No existing tests target `Feb 29`, leap years, or the newer 2038-style edge cases.

## Date/clock test helpers and fixtures

- **`Sources/AlmanacCore/Time/Clock.swift`** — the central injectable time abstraction:
  ```swift
  public protocol Clock: Sendable { var now: Date { get } }
  public struct SystemClock: Clock { public var now: Date { Date() } }
  public final class FixedClock: Clock, @unchecked Sendable {
      // lock-protected mutable `_now`, plus `set(_:)` and `advance(by:)`
  }
  ```
  Doc comment: *"Injectable time source. Every date in the core comes through this, so tests can pin 'now' and DST edges can be exercised deterministically."*
- `FixedClock` is the standard test fixture, almost always constructed as `FixedClock(Date(timeIntervalSince1970: 1_772_000_000))` (≈ 2026-02-25), used in `TimelineTests`, `ManualEntryTests`, `LaboratoryTests`, `ImportOrderingTests`, `HealthSyncTests`, `SyncAndBackupTests`. `advance(by:)` lets a test move time forward mid-test for anchor/failure-recovery scenarios.
- No dedicated fixed-`TimeZone`/`Calendar` injection helper class exists beyond passing `TimeZone(identifier:)` directly into `TimeModel.init` or `LabStore(..., zone: ZoneContext(...))`. No date-builder DSL — tests build ISO strings by hand (`PartialDateTime(text:precision:)`, or a local `instant(_ iso: String) -> Date` helper in `TimeModelTests` using `ISO8601DateFormatter`).

## Production date/time exposure (testability)

Good news for DST/timezone testing — there's real seam design:

- **`Clock` protocol** (above) is injected into stores (`LabStore(db:clock:...)`, `HealthSampleStore(..., clock:)`, `SyncAnchorStore(db:clock:)`, `LabCatalogStore(db:clock:)`), not called as bare `Date()`.
- **`TimeModel`** (`Sources/AlmanacCore/Time/TimeModel.swift`) wraps a `Calendar` with an explicit injected `TimeZone` and a `DayBoundary` (`.midnight` or `.wakeOffset(hours:)`); doc comment: *"All conversions go through Calendar with an explicit timezone, so DST transitions and non-Gregorian display calendars stay the calendar's problem rather than becoming arithmetic on 86,400."* Its `bounds(of:)` deliberately uses `calendar.date(byAdding: .day, value: 1, to: start)` rather than adding 86,400 seconds, specifically to get correct 23h/25h DST days.
- Only two direct `Date()` calls exist in production code (both are defaulted parameters, not hardcoded calls that bypass injection):
  - `Sources/AlmanacCore/Time/Clock.swift:11` — `SystemClock.now` itself (the intended real implementation).
  - `Sources/AlmanacCore/Time/PartialDateTime.swift:44` — `ZoneContext.init(_ timeZone:, at instant: Date = Date())` default parameter.
- `PartialDateTime`/`ZoneContext` (`Sources/AlmanacCore/Time/PartialDateTime.swift`) model precision-aware, offset-aware timestamps rather than raw `Date`, with `hasKnownOffset`, `span`, and `possibleSpan` (`PartialDateTimeSpan.swift`) explicitly reasoning about uncertainty windows (widened by `maxOffset = 14 * 3600` for unknown-offset values) — this is itself timezone-edge-case-aware design.

Overall: date/time logic is well-isolated behind `Clock` and `TimeModel`, so DST/timezone/leap-year test additions should be straightforward — inject a `TimeZone(identifier:)` into `TimeModel` and/or a `FixedClock` into a store, no monkey-patching needed.

## Ordering-aware imports / conflict resolution (reusable pattern for offline queue / sync recovery testing)

Git log confirms this work: `4b6f12e` "Manual-entry APIs, audited edits, ordering-aware imports, ambiguity-aware matching", `9928137` "fix: preserve laboratory revisions, conflicts and source ordering", `8836166` "feat: author native laboratory manual-entry interface".

Core files: **`Sources/AlmanacCore/Laboratory/LabSourceOrdering.swift`** (production) and **`Tests/AlmanacCoreTests/ImportOrderingTests.swift`** + **`RequestedFixTests.swift`** (tests).

Key types/patterns directly transferable to an offline queue / sync-recovery test suite:

- `SourceOrdering` enum (`.unavailable`, `.sequence(Int)`, `.issuedAt(String)`) with a `compare(to:) -> ComparisonResult?` that returns `nil` when two markers are **incomparable** (different kinds, or overlapping uncertainty windows) rather than guessing — this is the "can't tell what's newer" case a sync/queue test suite would also need.
- `UnrankedImportPolicy` (`.applyAndFlag` vs `.holdAsConflict`) — configurable strictness for what happens when incoming data can't be ranked against current state.
- Test scenarios in `ImportOrderingTests.swift` worth reusing as templates:
  - `testStaleReimportDoesNotBecomeCurrent` — replay of an old message after a newer one arrived is a no-op, idempotently, even replayed 3×.
  - `testExplicitRevertWithNewerOrderingIsAppliedNotTreatedAsReplay` — distinguishing a deliberate revert (ranked higher) from a stale replay (same content, no rank) — the same payload has to be treated differently based on ordering metadata, not content.

  - `testOrderingKindsMustMatchToRank` — asserts `nil` for incomparable ordering kinds (`.sequence` vs `.issuedAt`), and for `.unavailable` on either side.
  - `testUnrankedNewContentIsHeldAsAConflictUnderTheStrictPolicy` / `testExplicitApplyAndFlagOptInIsRecordedAsUnranked` — the two policy branches, each asserting on revision `.kind` (`"conflict"`, `"superseded_unranked"`).
- `RequestedFixTests.testDefaultConflictsCanBeAcceptedAndRejectedWithAudit` — conflict accept/reject flow with mandatory non-empty `reason`, audit columns (`resolved_by`, `resolution_reason`) queried directly via `db.query(...)`, and re-import-after-resolution idempotency (`hasUnresolvedConflict` stays `false`).
- Adjacent but simpler: `SyncAnchorStoreTests` in `SyncAndBackupTests.swift` — `testFailureKeepsLastGoodAnchor` (a failed sync must not clobber the last good cursor/token) and `testFakeHealthProviderRequiresAuthorisation`'s `"an empty batch must not reset the anchor"` assertion — both good small patterns for offline-queue "don't lose progress on failure" tests.
